To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the low palatability of leaves of Baccharus platypoda and the high concentration of lignocellulose in Coccoloba cerefera delayed the leaf decomposition process and reduced the participation of invertebrates.

the low palatability of leaves in a tropical stream, associated with low nutrient concentrations in water and high concentrations of tannins, delayed the leaf-conditioning process by microorganisms, reduced the breakdown rate, and reduced invertebrate participation in leaf decomposition.

i) leaf breakdown in a natural high-altitude tropical stream was slow; ii) the intrinsic factors of leaf litter (quality of detrius) may be more important than extrisic factors (microbial communities) in decomposition, and iii) low detrital quality hinders microbial colonisation, thereby altering the associated invertebrates communities and slows leaf breakdown.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of detrital inputs and associated organisms in the functioning of tropical headwater streams.
the importance of the quality of detritus in tropical stream decomposition, as well as the role of invertebrates and fungi in leaf breakdown.
the importance of leaf quality and the role of fungi as decomposers of low-quality litter in tropical stream ecosystems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the intrinsic factors of detritus are more important than the extrinsic factors in leaf decomposition, and the detritus quality may play a major role in the composition and structure invertebrate communities.
leaf quality, rather than decomposer communities, is the main factor determining the decomposition process in the studied tropical stream.
the decomposition process is a function of intrinsic and extrinsic factors, which act synergistically in the breakdown process of leaf litter in tropical streams.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the leaf breakdown of Baccharis and Coccoloba leaves in the present study was slow and was mainly driven by microbial processes.

the leaf quality and the microbial community associated with the litter play important roles in the leaf decomposition process, but the invertebrates associated to the detritus have a minor participation in the process.
the leaf quality is the main determinant for leaf decomposition and invertebrate colonization in the present study.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the decomposition of detrital resources in high-altitude streams is slow and that this process may be more dependent on physical processes than on the activity of microorganisms and invertebrates.
the quality and quantity of detritus in headwater streams are important for the functioning of aquatic food webs and the recycling of organic matter.
the decomposition process in tropical high-altitude streams is slow.
